response.text:
I need to decide what correction, if any, this finding warrants.

Finding F005 is a closed_period_posting. The fix convention says a correction must move affected accounts to their true position, but the finding itself is a control issue: a journal was posted to a closed period. Nothing in the evidence shows the amounts are wrong. The journal balances (DR 644.95 = CR 322.47 + 322.48 = 644.95). The accounts are valid and active. The period is closed, so moving the posting by reversing it into an open period would be a judgment the auditors should make, not something the data proves. Reposting into period 11 or 12 would also change the period-level results of a closed period without authorisation.

The correction must be small and only as the finding allows. The finding only says the posting needs authorisation review. It does not establish an error in the amounts, accounts, or balance. So the minimal and defensible action is no journal lines and no status changes, with the reasoning recorded for the reviewer. I'll submit an empty correction that references the original journal.

arguments.reasoning: Finding F005: GL journal 2470 (source GL, keyed by JSMITH, memo "Manual accrual") is dated 20241116 and posted to PRD_ID 10, which closed on 20241105. The evidence shows a timing/authorisation control exception, not a data error. The journal balances (DR 644.95 = CR 322.47 + CR 322.48), all three accounts (5200, 2100, 1200) are valid and active, and the amounts are internally consistent. No amount, account, or balance error is evident, so no correcting journal lines are proposed. Moving the entry into open period 11 or 12 would change the results of a closed period and would need authorisation first, so I have not done that. No invoice status is changed, since this is not a duplicate invoice. Recommended action: have the period-10 owner confirm whether the post-close entry was authorised and, if it was not, decide between reversing it and re-posting it in an open period, as a separate approved correction.
